attachments.origin_landmark: oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and the side of the cricoid (the laryngeal cartilages are not modeled as skeletal elements in this pass -- approximated via the adjacent hyoid attachment region)

actions: its cricopharyngeus part acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter

functional_compartments.name: Thyropharyngeus (oblique part)
functional_compartments.function_note: Oblique fibres from the thyroid cartilage. Killian's dehiscence -- the weak triangle between these oblique fibres and the transverse cricopharyngeus below -- is where a Zenker's pharyngeal pouch herniates.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

functional_compartments.name: Cricopharyngeus (transverse part)
functional_compartments.function_note: Transverse fibres from the cricoid, tonically contracted as the upper oesophageal sphincter and relaxing to admit the bolus. Failure of that relaxation is the mechanism behind Zenker's diverticulum, and the target of cricopharyngeal myotomy.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Not an ultrasound-guided technique in standard clinical use -- the cricopharyngeus (transverse) part is targeted percutaneously under EMG guidance. Two described approaches: (1) trans-cricothyroid-membrane -- needle enters through the cricothyroid membrane in the midline and is advanced posteriorly through the airway lumen, the posterior cricoid plate and the posterior cricoarytenoid muscles to reach the cricopharyngeus from behind; (2) lateral transcervical -- needle inserted at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the mid-level of the cricoid cartilage, or per Ertekin et al. about 1.5 cm lateral to the palpable lateral border of the cricoid cartilage. The thyropharyngeus (oblique) part is not separately targeted in the reviewed literature; a single percutaneous injection into the inferior constrictor mass (not further localized to thyropharyngeus vs cricopharyngeus) has also been described for post-laryngectomy pharyngoesophageal (PE) segment spasm.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Cricopharyngeus lies posterior to the cricoid lamina and posterior cricoarytenoid muscles; for the trans-cricothyroid route the needle traverses skin, cricothyroid membrane, subglottic airway lumen, posterior cricoid plate and posterior cricoarytenoid muscle before reaching the cricopharyngeus.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: EMG confirms cricopharyngeus placement: tonic resting activity that drops out during swallowing followed by a rapid burst, then a return to baseline. The patient is asked to sniff to activate the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (a burst of EMG signal on sniff means the needle is in PCA, not cricopharyngeus, and should be repositioned).
structures_at_risk: posterior cricoarytenoid muscle -- inadvertent injection/diffusion causes transient noisy breathing or dyspnea on exertion (reported in ~39% of an EMG-guided percutaneous case series)
recurrent laryngeal nerve and vocal fold function -- one case series reported a single instance of transient unilateral vocal fold paralysis
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Two distinct indications drive this literature: (1) retrograde cricopharyngeal dysfunction / inability to burp (R-CPD) -- most commonly treated endoscopically via esophagoscopy under general anesthesia (50-100 U), with EMG-guided percutaneous in-office injection (50-75 U, half per side) as a growing alternative; meta-analysis found endoscopic injection had higher early success than percutaneous EMG-guided injection, with higher doses (up to 100 U) giving better sustained relief; (2) classic cricopharyngeal achalasia / UES hyperactivity causing oropharyngeal dysphagia (post-stroke, ALS, diabetic neuropathy, pediatric) -- treated by percutaneous EMG-guided, CT-guided, or endoscopic injection, typically 10-100 U depending on age/etiology. This is a genuinely EMG- or endoscope-guided procedure in the reviewed literature, not an ultrasound-guided one -- flagged here per the field's intended use for non-ultrasound techniques.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Wajsberg B, Hoesli RC, Wingo ML, Bastian RW, 'Efficacy and Safety of Electromyography-Guided Injection of Botulinum Toxin to Treat Retrograde Cricopharyngeus Dysfunction', OTO Open 5(1):2473974X21989587 (2021), doi:10.1177/2473974X21989587 -- describes the trans-cricothyroid-membrane technique and cites Ertekin et al.'s lateral percutaneous landmark (~1.5cm lateral to the cricoid's palpable lateral border); Kim MS, Kim GW, Rho YS, Kwon KH, Chung EJ, 'Office-based Electromyography-guided Botulinum Toxin Injection to the Cricopharyngeus Muscle: Optimal Patient Selection and Technique', Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 126(5):349-356 (2017), doi:10.1177/0003489416689469; Yeo WX, Tan BKJ, Gao EY, Yeap SYY, Leong ZH, 'Botulinum Toxin Injection in Retrograde Cricopharyngeal Dysfunction: A Meta-Analysis', Laryngoscope 135(11):4030-4041 (2025), doi:10.1002/lary.32296; Hoesli RC, Wingo ML, Bastian RW, 'The Long-term Efficacy of Botulinum Toxin Injection to Treat Retrograde Cricopharyngeus Dysfunction', OTO Open 4(2):2473974X20938342 (2020), doi:10.1177/2473974X20938342; Bartolomei L, Zambito Marsala S, Pighi GP, et al., 'Botulinum toxin type A: an effective treatment to restore phonation in laryngectomized patients unable to voice', Neurol Sci 32(3):443-447 (2011), doi:10.1007/s10072-011-0560-1 (percutaneous EMG-guided injection into the middle/inferior pharyngeal constrictor mass for pharyngoesophageal segment spasm) -- all retrieved via PubMed.
